stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
For much of the twentieth century, ecologists treated the forest floor as a passive recipient of whatever fell from the canopy: leaves, branches and the occasional carcass, all broken down at a pace set by temperature and moisture. Studies of decomposition accordingly focused on climate, and models predicted that leaf litter would decay at similar rates in any two forests with similar weather.

Field results repeatedly defied those predictions. Litter from the same tree species, placed in different forests with nearly identical climates, decayed at markedly different rates. One explanation, now called the home-field advantage hypothesis, holds that the fungi and bacteria beneath a given tree species become specialized in breaking down that species' litter. Transplanted litter, on this view, decays slowly not because the new site is colder or drier but because the local decomposers are unaccustomed to it. The hypothesis does not dismiss climate; rather, it suggests that climate sets the outer limits of decomposition while the history of a site determines where within those limits the actual rate falls.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: Historians of the book have long assumed that the shift from manuscript to print in fifteenth-century Europe was abrupt: once presses spread, scribes lost their trade within a generation. Surviving account books from several monasteries tell a more gradual story. Scribes continued to be paid for copying well into the sixteenth century, and some printed books were deliberately finished by hand, with painted initials and margins designed to resemble those of manuscripts. Buyers, it seems, did not regard the two technologies as rivals. A wealthy patron might even commission a handwritten copy of a text precisely because printed versions had made that text widely available, and therefore unremarkable.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Economists have long noted that people often value an object more once they own it, a pattern called the endowment effect. In a typical experiment, half the participants receive a mug and are asked the lowest price at which they would sell it; the other half are asked the highest price they would pay for the same mug. Sellers' prices are commonly about twice as high as buyers'. The standard explanation is loss aversion: giving up something one owns feels like a loss, and losses weigh more heavily than equivalent gains.

Later research added a qualification. When goods are held for exchange rather than for use, as when a shop owner sells stock or a trader sells shares, the effect largely disappears. A dealer does not mourn each sale. This finding suggests that the endowment effect depends less on ownership itself than on how the owner expects to use what is owned.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: Coral reefs are often described as fragile, and in one sense they are: a few weeks of unusually warm water can cause corals to expel the algae that live in their tissues and supply most of their food, leaving the corals white and starving. Yet bleaching is not always fatal. If temperatures fall quickly enough, many corals take up algae again and recover. Some researchers now study reefs that have survived repeated bleaching, hoping to learn whether the corals there host heat-tolerant algae or have themselves become more resistant.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Literary historians have tended to read the explosion of travel writing in eighteenth-century Britain as evidence of a newly curious public, eager for knowledge of distant places. The sheer number of travel books seems to support this view: by some counts, they outsold every category except religious works. Yet a closer look at how such books were produced complicates the picture. Many were compiled by writers who had never left England, stitched together from earlier accounts and reissued under new titles with little revision. Publishers, it appears, were responding less to a demand for new information than to a demand for a familiar kind of reading pleasure: the narrative of a journey, with its promise of hardship overcome and its comfortable return home.

None of this means readers were incurious. But it suggests that the popularity of a genre is weak evidence of the motives of its audience. A book can sell because it confirms expectations as readily as because it challenges them, and the travel book, in its most commercial forms, seems to have done more of the former than the latter.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: Many plants that flower in early spring, before the trees above them leaf out, are pollinated by queen bumblebees, which emerge from hibernation in the same weeks. Because flowering is triggered largely by temperature and bee emergence partly by day length, warming springs have prompted concern that the two events could drift apart, leaving early flowers unvisited. Records from one long-studied meadow suggest the concern is partly warranted: over forty years, the flowers there have advanced by about two weeks, the bees by only one. Yet seed production in the meadow has not declined, perhaps because late-season visits by other insects make up some of the difference.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: When the first public lending libraries opened in British industrial towns in the 1850s, their founders described them as instruments of improvement: workers who read history and science, it was hoped, would become sober, skilled and content. Borrowing records from the period show that readers had other ideas. Fiction made up well over half of all loans at most libraries, and serialized adventure stories were among the most requested titles. Some library committees responded by limiting their purchases of novels; others decided that any reading was better than none and bought what was asked for. The records thus document not only what workers read but a running negotiation between the people who ran the libraries and the people who used them.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: Most mammals stop producing lactase, the enzyme that digests the sugar in milk, soon after weaning. In some human populations, however, lactase production continues into adulthood, a trait known as lactase persistence. Genetic studies have found that the trait arose independently in several regions, through different mutations, in each case among peoples with a long history of herding cattle, goats or camels. The pattern is a textbook example of convergent evolution: similar pressures produced similar outcomes by different routes. What the pressure was remains debated. Milk supplies calories, fat and protein, but in some dry regions it may also have been valued as a source of clean water, and researchers disagree about which benefit mattered most.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
Urban planners once assumed that wider roads would ease congestion. Experience suggested otherwise. Within a few years of a major highway's expansion, traffic often returned to its earlier levels, a pattern known as induced demand. The extra capacity made driving faster for a while, and people responded by driving more: taking trips they would otherwise have skipped, choosing more distant jobs or homes, or switching from buses and trains to cars.

The same logic can run in reverse. When a road is closed or narrowed, some of its traffic does not reappear elsewhere but simply vanishes, as people combine errands, travel at other times or stop making certain trips. Planners in several cities have used this finding to justify converting traffic lanes into bus lanes or space for pedestrians, with less disruption than critics predicted.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: The octopus has a large nervous system for an invertebrate, but most of its neurons are not in its brain. About two thirds lie in its eight arms, which can carry out complex movements with little direction from the center: an arm separated from the body will still reach for food and pass it toward where the mouth would be. Researchers describe the arrangement as distributed control. The brain sets general goals, such as reaching for a crab, while each arm works out the details of how to bend and grasp.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text:
The standard history of photography treats its early decades as a contest between art and science. In one camp stood those who saw the camera as a mechanical recorder of facts, useful to astronomers and surveyors; in the other, those who insisted that a photograph could be composed, lit and printed with as much intention as a painting. The story ends, conventionally, with the triumph of the second camp and photography's admission to museums.

Recent scholarship has questioned whether the two camps were ever as distinct as this account suggests. Many of the same practitioners produced both scientific plates and exhibition prints, and techniques moved freely between the two: methods developed for photographing faint stars, for example, were adapted by portraitists seeking softer light. The rivalry, on this view, was largely a creation of later critics, who needed a narrative in which photography had to earn its status as art. That need says more about the critics' own debates than about the medium's early practice.

stimuli.title: Passage
stimuli.text: Because volcanoes release carbon dioxide, one might expect eruptions to warm the planet. Large explosive eruptions, however, can cool it for several years. They inject sulfur gases high into the stratosphere, where the gases form tiny droplets that reflect sunlight before it reaches the surface. Because the stratosphere has no rain to wash the droplets out, they can linger for two or three years, far longer than particles in the lower atmosphere. The carbon dioxide from such an eruption, by contrast, is small compared with what human activity releases each year, so its warming effect is minor.

questions.stem: Although the committee's report was meant to settle the dispute, its conclusions were so _____ that each faction claimed the document supported its own position.
questions.explanation: If every faction can read the report as supporting its own side, the conclusions must be open to more than one reading: equivocal. An incisive report would cut through the dispute and favor one side, the opposite of what happened.

questions.stem: The biographer resists the temptation to _____ her subject, a man she plainly admires; she records his pettiness as carefully as his generosity.
questions.explanation: An admiring biographer's temptation is to idealize, and recording his faults resists exactly that: lionize. Disparage is a one-sided treatment too, but it is not a temptation for someone who admires her subject.

questions.stem: Early reviewers dismissed the novel as [[1]], a light entertainment with nothing to say; only decades later did critics recognize the [[2]] social commentary concealed beneath its comic surface.
questions.explanation: "A light entertainment with nothing to say" defines the first blank: frivolous (didactic means preachy, the opposite). The later critics found real commentary, so the second blank needs a word of praise: trenchant, meaning sharp and incisive. Superficial would repeat the early reviewers' judgment.

questions.stem: The new regulations were intended to [[1]] the approval process for small builders, but in practice they had the opposite effect: the paperwork they required was so [[2]] that many applicants simply abandoned their projects, and the backlog the rules were meant to clear [[3]].
questions.explanation: "The opposite effect" of slowing builders down means the intent was to streamline. Paperwork that made applicants give up was onerous, not perfunctory. And if the rules backfired, the backlog they were meant to clear grew rather than vanished.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: comparing the field methods of two rival groups of ecologists
describing findings that complicated an earlier view and presenting an explanation for them
explaining why ecologists abandoned models of decomposition
defending a traditional model of decomposition against evidence that appears to contradict it
arguing that climate has little effect on the rate of decomposition
questions.explanation: The passage sets out the climate-centered view, reports field results that defied it and offers the home-field advantage hypothesis to explain them. It says explicitly that the hypothesis does not dismiss climate, so the claim that climate has little effect misreads the last sentence.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about the home-field advantage hypothesis? Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.
options: It predicts that litter placed beneath its own tree species decays faster than the same litter placed beneath another species in a similar climate.
It holds that the decomposers at a site reflect the tree species that have grown there.
It implies that forests with different climates will show the same rates of decay.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis says local decomposers specialize in the litter of the trees above them, so litter decays faster at home than when transplanted and the decomposer community reflects the site's history of tree species. It keeps climate as the outer limit on decomposition, so it does not predict equal decay across different climates.

questions.stem:
Despite the senator's reputation for _____, her speech to the convention was brief and plain, free of the flourishes her critics had come to expect.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: "Despite" sets up a contrast with a brief, plain speech, so her reputation is for inflated, showy language: grandiloquence and bombast. Brevity and terseness are a matching pair, but they describe the speech itself and remove the contrast.

questions.stem:
The researcher's findings, initially greeted with skepticism, were eventually _____ by a series of independent studies that reproduced her results in different populations.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Studies that reproduced her results confirmed them: corroborated and substantiated. Refuted and undermined are a pair but contradict "reproduced her results"; anticipated and publicized have no partner with the same meaning.

questions.stem:
Far from being _____, the director's decisions on set were the product of long deliberation, though they often seemed sudden to the actors who received them.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: "Far from" contrasts the blank with long deliberation, so the decisions were not made on a whim: impulsive and capricious. Methodical and considered describe what the decisions actually were, which destroys the contrast.

questions.passage: Last year the city of Varden installed security cameras at its main train station. In the following year, the number of bicycle thefts reported at the station fell by 30 percent. City council members concluded that the cameras deterred thieves, and they have proposed installing cameras at every station in the city.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the council members' conclusion?
options: Several residents objected to the cameras on the grounds that they record people without their consent.
At the time the cameras were installed, the station's open racks were replaced with lockers that open only with a key card.
The number of people who own bicycles in Varden rose slightly during the year after the cameras went up, according to a city survey.
The cameras cost less to install and run than the council had originally estimated they would.
Before the cameras were installed, most bicycle thefts in Varden took place at the main train station.
questions.explanation: Key-card lockers offer another explanation for the drop in thefts, so the cameras may not be the cause. A rise in bicycle ownership would, if anything, make the fall in thefts more impressive, and the other choices do not bear on whether the cameras caused the decline.

questions.stem: The author mentions painted initials and margins primarily in order to
options: illustrate that early printed books borrowed features of manuscripts instead of simply displacing them
explain why the monasteries kept such detailed account books in this period
show that early printers lacked the skill to decorate the books they produced
suggest that scribes actively resisted the spread of printing presses
argue that hand-finished printed books were valued more highly by buyers than any of the surviving manuscripts
questions.explanation: The detail supports the claim that buyers did not see print and manuscript as rivals: printed books were made to look like manuscripts. Nothing in the passage says printers lacked skill; the hand finishing was deliberate.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage suggests which of the following about some wealthy patrons?
options: They could not afford printed books and therefore turned to monastery scribes for copies instead.
They commissioned scribes mainly in order to support the monasteries.
They preferred to collect texts that had never been printed at all.
They valued a handwritten copy partly because it set them apart from owners of printed copies.
They distrusted the accuracy of texts that had been produced on a press.
questions.explanation: A patron wanted a handwritten copy because print had made the text common and "unremarkable", so the handwritten copy marked its owner out. The patrons were wealthy, and the sentence concerns texts that had been printed, so the cost and never-printed readings contradict it.

questions.stem: The hikers had expected the trail to be crowded, but on that rainy weekday it was almost entirely _____.
questions.explanation: "But" contrasts with the expected crowds, so the trail was empty: deserted. Congested repeats the expectation instead of contrasting with it.

questions.stem: Because the instructions were written in clear, everyday language, even first-time users found the device remarkably _____ to set up.
questions.explanation: Clear instructions make setup easy: straightforward. Tedious and cumbersome describe the opposite of what clear instructions produce.

questions.stem: The mayor's critics called her plan _____, arguing that it promised far more than the city's budget could ever deliver.
questions.explanation: A plan that promises more than the budget can deliver is unrealistic. Modest and cautious plans promise little, the opposite of the critics' complaint.

questions.stem: The team's early success proved [[1]]: after winning its first six games, it lost nine of the next ten, and by midseason its fans had grown [[2]].
questions.explanation: Six wins followed by nine losses in ten means the success did not last: short-lived. Fans who watched that collapse would be disillusioned, not jubilant.

questions.stem: Unlike her [[1]] predecessor, who rarely spoke to reporters, the new director [[2]] the press, holding weekly briefings and answering questions at length.
questions.explanation: A predecessor who rarely spoke to reporters was reclusive (garrulous means talkative). "Unlike" signals that the new director did the reverse, seeking out the press: courted.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly concerned with
options: showing that loss aversion has no role in the endowment effect
arguing that people should value their possessions less than they do
comparing the pricing habits of shop owners with those of traders
criticizing economists for relying on simple laboratory experiments with cheap, ordinary objects like mugs
explaining a pattern in how people value objects and qualifying an account of when it occurs
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes the endowment effect and its usual explanation; the second adds a qualification about goods held for exchange. The passage never says loss aversion plays no role, only that the effect depends on the expected use of the goods.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in the typical mug experiment, the participants who received a mug
options: valued the mugs less than participants who had not received one
refused to sell their mugs at any price the buyers offered to pay
behaved much as shop owners do when selling their stock
named prices close to what they believed the same mug would cost to buy in an ordinary shop
named selling prices about twice as high as the prices other participants would pay
questions.explanation: The passage states that sellers' prices are commonly about twice as high as buyers'. It says nothing about outright refusals, and the comparison with shop owners is the qualification, not the typical result.

questions.stem: The author mentions a dealer who "does not mourn each sale" primarily in order to
options: show that the mug experiment was poorly designed and should be repeated
illustrate why the effect weakens for goods that are held to be exchanged
argue that the endowment effect is strongest among professional traders
explain why buyers usually offer less than sellers ask for an object
suggest that dealers are less loss averse than other people in general
questions.explanation: The dealer sells stock held for exchange, so parting with it is not felt as a loss; that is why the effect largely disappears for such goods. The passage ties the difference to how goods are used, not to dealers being a different kind of person.

questions.stem:
The guide's directions were so _____ that the group took three wrong turns before reaching the lake.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Directions that led to three wrong turns lacked clarity: vague and imprecise. Detailed and thorough are a pair but would not explain getting lost.

questions.stem:
Though the speaker began nervously, she grew more _____ as the audience responded warmly to her opening jokes.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: "Though she began nervously" sets up the change to the opposite: confident and assured. Hesitant and timid are a pair but continue the nervousness instead of contrasting with it.

questions.stem:
The museum's new wing, praised for its restraint, is a(n) _____ building: plain walls, few windows and almost no ornament.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Plain walls and no ornament describe a severe, unadorned building: austere and spartan. Ornate and lavish form a pair with the opposite meaning.

questions.passage: Employees at Halvern Corporation may choose to work from home two days a week. A survey found that employees who made that choice reported higher job satisfaction than employees who worked in the office every day. Halvern's managers concluded that allowing more remote work would raise job satisfaction across the company.
questions.stem: The managers' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Job satisfaction is the single most important influence on how productive an employee is at Halvern.
The employees who chose remote work were not already more satisfied before working from home.
Allowing more remote work would reduce the amount Halvern spends on renting and running offices.
Most employees at Halvern would prefer to work from home on every working day of the week.
Employees who work in the office every day tend to work longer hours than those who work from home.
questions.explanation: Because employees chose remote work, the satisfied ones may simply be the kind who choose it; the conclusion needs the satisfaction to come from remote work, not the other way round. The managers need not assume that most employees want full-time remote work: the argument is about more remote work, not all of it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, bleached corals appear white because they
options: have expelled the algae that normally live in their tissues
have taken up algae that tolerate unusually warm water
have stopped growing during several weeks of warm water
have been killed by a sudden fall in water temperature
have been covered by sediment stirred up by storms
questions.explanation: The first sentence says warm water causes corals to expel their algae, "leaving the corals white". Cooling is described as what lets corals recover, not as the cause of bleaching.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about corals is supported by the passage? Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.
options: Bleaching almost always kills the corals that it affects.
Whether a bleached coral survives can depend on how long high temperatures last.
Corals depend on the algae in their tissues for much of their food.
questions.explanation: Corals recover "if temperatures fall quickly enough", so the length of the warm spell matters, and the algae "supply most of their food". The passage says bleaching "is not always fatal" and that many corals recover, which contradicts the claim that bleaching almost always kills.

questions.passage: The managers of a city park planted native wildflowers along one of its two jogging paths. The following summer, volunteers counted twice as many bees along the planted path as along the unplanted one. The managers concluded that the wildflowers attracted the additional bees.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the managers' conclusion?
options: Bees in the region are generally more active in the summer than they are in the spring.
The planted path has become noticeably more popular with joggers and walkers than the unplanted path.
Before the planting, volunteers had counted about the same number of bees along both paths.
The volunteers counted bees along the paths on only three days during the summer.
Some of the wildflowers that were planted bloom only for a few weeks each summer.
questions.explanation: If the paths had equal bee counts before the planting, the planting is the likely cause of the difference afterward. Seasonal activity affects both paths equally, and the three-day count, if anything, weakens confidence in the result.

questions.stem: The scientist's prose is anything but _____: every sentence is so freighted with qualification and technical aside that even specialists find her papers slow going.
questions.explanation: "Anything but" reverses the blank: her prose is dense and hard going, so it is anything but clear, which is limpid. Abstruse and prolix describe what her prose actually is, so they would make the sentence contradict itself.

questions.stem: Critics who expected the retrospective to _____ the painter's reputation were surprised: the exhibition, by placing his minor works beside his acknowledged masterpieces, made his achievement seem more rather than less substantial.
questions.explanation: The critics were surprised because his achievement seemed greater, so they had expected the show to damage his reputation: tarnish. Burnish and cement name the outcome that actually occurred, so there would be no surprise.

questions.stem: The essayist's apparent [[1]] is deceptive; beneath the casual tone and offhand jokes lies an argument so carefully [[2]] that no paragraph could be removed without weakening the whole.
questions.explanation: A casual tone and offhand jokes suggest carefree unconcern: insouciance. The "deceptive" surface hides an argument in which every paragraph is needed, so it is carefully constructed, not improvised.

questions.stem: For decades the theory enjoyed a(n) [[1]] status in its field, less because its predictions had been confirmed than because no rival had been proposed. When an alternative finally appeared, the old theory's defenders, rather than [[2]] its weaknesses, [[3]] them, insisting that the anomalies were errors of measurement.
questions.explanation: With no rival, the theory dominated: hegemonic. Insisting that anomalies were measurement errors is a way of explaining the weaknesses away, which is the opposite of conceding them, as "rather than" requires.

questions.stem: Though the treaty was hailed as a(n) [[1]] achievement, its provisions were in fact so [[2]] that each signatory could interpret them as permitting exactly what it had intended to do anyway.
questions.explanation: "Though" contrasts lavish praise with the reality, so it was hailed as a landmark. Provisions that let each party read them however it liked were elastic; stringent or precise provisions would constrain the signatories.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view described in the first sentence is best described as one of
questions.explanation: The author doubts that sales show curiosity ("weak evidence") but adds "None of this means readers were incurious", a qualified rather than total rejection. Dismissive contempt ignores that concession.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim about what publishers were responding to?
options: Religious works outsold travel books in nearly every year of the eighteenth century.
Many of the most popular travel books were reissued in cheaper editions in the last decades of the century.
Readers of travel books also bought large numbers of novels about domestic life.
Some travel books of the period were written by authors who had traveled widely abroad.
Travel books compiled from earlier accounts sold far fewer copies than those based on new journeys.
questions.explanation: The author infers from recycled content that publishers were not chasing new information. If recycled books sold poorly and books from new journeys sold well, readers evidently did want new information. That some authors traveled is consistent with the author's claim that many did not.

questions.stem: The passage suggests which of the following about eighteenth-century travel books? Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.
options: Their sales alone do not establish why readers bought them.
Some presented recycled material as though it were new.
They were read chiefly by people planning journeys of their own.
questions.explanation: Books "reissued under new titles with little revision" passed off old material as new, and the author says popularity is "weak evidence of the motives of its audience". Nothing suggests readers were planning journeys; the passage stresses the pleasure of reading about a journey.

questions.stem:
The reviewer's praise was so _____ that the author could not tell whether she had been complimented or mocked.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: If the author could not tell compliment from mockery, the praise allowed two readings: equivocal and ambiguous. Lavish and unstinting are a pair, but generous praise leaves no doubt.

questions.stem:
Although the policy was presented as a bold departure, close observers saw it as merely _____, a slight adjustment to practices that had been in place for years.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: "A slight adjustment" defines the blank: incremental and marginal both mean a small change. Radical and revolutionary match the official description the observers rejected.

questions.stem:
The archive's holdings are vast but _____: letters written in the same month may be stored in a dozen different boxes, with no index to connect them.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Related letters scattered across boxes with no index describe disorder: haphazard and chaotic. Meticulous and systematic are a pair with the opposite meaning, and voluminous merely repeats "vast".

questions.passage: Over the past decade, the share of adults in Lestonia who hold a university degree has risen from 22 percent to 31 percent, while the average wage of workers with a degree has stayed flat after adjusting for inflation. Some analysts argue that the growing supply of graduates has reduced the economic value of a degree.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analysts' argument?
options: Some graduates in Lestonia work in jobs that do not require a university degree.
Over the same decade, the average real wage of workers without a degree fell by 12 percent.
The number of universities in Lestonia increased during the decade, mostly in its largest cities.
Tuition at Lestonian universities rose faster than inflation for most of the decade.
Most of the new graduates studied subjects whose graduates have historically earned low wages.
questions.explanation: The value of a degree is what it adds over not having one. If non-graduate wages fell while graduate wages held steady, the gap widened, so a degree became worth more, not less. The choice about low-wage subjects offers an explanation for flat wages that is compatible with the analysts' view.

questions.passage: {{Ice cores drilled from Greenland's glaciers have long served as archives of past climate.}} {{Each year's snowfall traps tiny bubbles of air, and the chemistry of the surrounding ice records the temperature at which the snow formed.}} {{Until recently, however, the record of the last few centuries was considered unreliable, because the uppermost layers are compacted unevenly as new snow accumulates.}} {{A new method that counts annual layers by their dust content has allowed researchers to date even these upper layers to within a year or two.}} {{The method's accuracy was confirmed when it placed the ash from a well-documented eruption in exactly the year the eruption was recorded.}}
questions.stem: Select the sentence in the passage that presents evidence that a new technique works as intended.
questions.explanation: The last sentence reports a check against a known date: the method put the eruption's ash in the recorded year. The fourth sentence describes what the method does but offers no evidence that it is accurate.

questions.stem: The information about seed production in the last sentence serves primarily to
options: suggest that bumblebees are no longer needed to pollinate early flowers
provide evidence that the records from the meadow are unreliable
show that the concern about warming springs was unfounded from the start
explain why flowers have advanced their blooming more than bees
indicate that a predicted consequence has not yet followed from an observed change
questions.explanation: The flowers and bees have drifted apart, as feared, but the expected result, fewer seeds, has not appeared. The author calls the concern "partly warranted", so the sentence does not show it was unfounded.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that if bee emergence were triggered entirely by temperature, then
options: flowers would no longer depend on other insects for late-season visits
the timing of flowering and of bee emergence would be less likely to drift apart as springs warm
warming springs would delay the emergence of queen bumblebees
bees would emerge before the trees above the meadow plants leaf out
seed production in the meadow would begin to decline as late-season insect visits became less frequent
questions.explanation: The risk of drift comes from the two events having different triggers: temperature for flowers, partly day length for bees. If both responded to temperature alone, they would tend to shift together. Warming would make temperature-triggered bees emerge earlier, not later.

questions.stem:
**Quantity A:** $\frac{3}{8}$

**Quantity B:** $0.4$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $\frac{3}{8} = 0.375$, which is less than $0.4$, so Quantity B is greater.

questions.stem:
$x > 0$

**Quantity A:** $x^2$

**Quantity B:** $x$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: If $x = 2$, then $x^2 = 4 > 2$; if $x = \frac{1}{2}$, then $x^2 = \frac{1}{4} < \frac{1}{2}$; if $x = 1$ they are equal. Positive is not enough to decide.

questions.stem:
A rectangle that is not a square has a perimeter of $20$.

**Quantity A:** The area of the rectangle

**Quantity B:** $25$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Length plus width is $10$. The area $lw$ is greatest when $l = w = 5$, giving $25$, but that is a square. For any other rectangle, such as $6 \times 4 = 24$, the area is less than $25$.

questions.stem:
$S = \{3, 5, 7, 9, 21\}$

**Quantity A:** The mean of the numbers in $S$

**Quantity B:** The median of the numbers in $S$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The sum is $3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 21 = 45$, so the mean is $9$. The median is the middle value, $7$. The large value $21$ pulls the mean above the median.

questions.stem: A jacket priced at \$80 is discounted 25 percent, and the discounted price is then reduced by a further 10 percent. What is the final price of the jacket?
questions.explanation: After 25 percent off: $80 \times 0.75 = 60$. After a further 10 percent: $60 \times 0.9 = 54$. Taking 35 percent off at once (\$52) is wrong because the second discount applies to the reduced price.

questions.stem: If $3x - 7 = 2x + 5$, what is the value of $x^2$?
questions.explanation: Subtract $2x$ and add $7$: $x = 12$, so $x^2 = 144$. A sign error ($x = -2$, from adding the wrong way) leads to $4$.

questions.stem: The two legs of a right triangle have lengths 9 and 12. What is the length of the hypotenuse? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: $9^2 + 12^2 = 81 + 144 = 225$, and $\sqrt{225} = 15$. This is the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 3.

questions.stem: Which of the following integers are divisors of 84? Indicate all such integers.
questions.explanation: $84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$. Its divisors include $6$, $12$ and $14$. A divisor can contain at most two factors of 2, so $8 = 2^3$ and $16 = 2^4$ do not divide it.

questions.stem:
The table shows how many books each of 20 students read last month.

| Books read | Number of students |
|---|---|
| 0 | 2 |
| 1 | 5 |
| 2 | 6 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 4 | 3 |

What is the median number of books read?
questions.explanation: With 20 values the median is the average of the 10th and 11th. The first 2 values are 0, the next 5 (3rd to 7th) are 1 and the next 6 (8th to 13th) are 2, so both middle values are 2.

questions.stem: A bag contains 4 red, 5 blue and 3 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are blue?
questions.explanation: $P = \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{4}{11} = \frac{20}{132} = \frac{5}{33}$. Replacing the first marble would give $\frac{25}{144}$, which is the wrong model here.

questions.stem: Working alone at a constant rate, one pump fills a tank in 6 hours. A second pump, working alone at a constant rate, fills the same tank in 3 hours. How many hours do the two pumps take to fill the tank working together?
questions.explanation: Rates add: $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$ tank per hour, so the tank takes $2$ hours. Averaging the times ($4.5$) ignores that the faster pump does more of the work.

questions.stem: A circle has a circumference of $10\pi$. What is its area?
questions.explanation: $2\pi r = 10\pi$ gives $r = 5$, so the area is $\pi r^2 = 25\pi$. Using the diameter $10$ as the radius gives $100\pi$.

questions.stem:
**Quantity A:** 20% of 45

**Quantity B:** 45% of 18

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $0.2 \times 45 = 9$ and $0.45 \times 18 = 8.1$, so Quantity A is greater.

questions.stem:
$y = 2x + 3$ and $x = 4$

**Quantity A:** $y$

**Quantity B:** $12$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $y = 2(4) + 3 = 11$, which is less than $12$.

questions.stem:
Two angles of a triangle measure $50^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.

**Quantity A:** The measure of the third angle, in degrees

**Quantity B:** $65$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The angles of a triangle sum to $180$, so the third angle is $180 - 50 - 60 = 70$, which is greater than $65$.

questions.stem:
A list of five integers has a mean of $6$.

**Quantity A:** The sum of the five integers

**Quantity B:** $30$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Sum $=$ mean $\times$ count $= 6 \times 5 = 30$, whatever the integers are.

questions.stem:
$n$ is an integer and $3 < n < 7$.

**Quantity A:** $n$

**Quantity B:** $5$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $n$ can be $4$, $5$ or $6$, so $n$ can be less than, equal to or greater than $5$.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of sugar. How many cups of sugar are needed with 12 cups of flour?
questions.explanation: 12 cups of flour is 4 times 3, so use $4 \times 2 = 8$ cups of sugar. 18 comes from scaling the ratio the wrong way round.

questions.stem: What is 40 percent of 35? Type the number only.
The average (arithmetic mean) of 4, 7, 10 and $x$ is 8. What is the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: The four numbers must sum to $4 \times 8 = 32$. $4 + 7 + 10 = 21$, so $x = 11$.

questions.stem: A rectangle has length 8 and width 5. What is the length of its diagonal?
questions.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 5: $\sqrt{64 + 25} = \sqrt{89}$. Adding the sides ($13$) is not how a diagonal works.

questions.stem: Five test scores are 72, 85, 90, 78 and 85. What is the range of the scores?
questions.explanation: Range $=$ greatest $-$ least $= 90 - 72 = 18$. $82$ is the mean and $85$ is the mode.

questions.stem: Which of the following values of $x$ satisfy $x^2 < 9$? Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: $x^2 < 9$ means $-3 < x < 3$. $-2$, $0$ and $2.5$ qualify; $3^2 = 9$ is not less than 9, and $(-4)^2 = 16$.

questions.stem: A store's weekly sales rose from \$400 to \$500. By what percent did the sales increase?
questions.explanation: Percent change $= \frac{500 - 400}{400} = \frac{100}{400} = 25\%$. Dividing by the new value gives the 20 percent trap.

questions.stem: A cube has a volume of 64 cubic centimeters. What is its total surface area, in square centimeters? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Each edge is $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$, each face has area $16$ and a cube has 6 faces: $6 \times 16 = 96$.

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, 18 play soccer, 12 play basketball and 5 play both. How many students play neither sport?
questions.explanation: Students who play at least one sport: $18 + 12 - 5 = 25$. Neither: $30 - 25 = 5$. Forgetting to subtract the overlap gives $0$.

questions.stem: Museum tickets cost \$8 for adults and \$5 for children. A group of 10 people paid \$62 in all. How many adults were in the group?

**Quantity A:** $(0.9)^{10}$

**Quantity B:** $0.9$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Multiplying a positive number by $0.9$ makes it smaller, so $(0.9)^{10}$ is less than $0.9$ (about $0.35$).

questions.stem:
$xy < 0$ and $x > y$

**Quantity A:** $x$

**Quantity B:** $0$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $xy < 0$ means one is positive and the other negative. Since $x > y$, $x$ is the positive one, so $x > 0$.

questions.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 5$ and $BC = 8$.

**Quantity A:** The length of $AC$

**Quantity B:** $13$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: In any triangle a side is shorter than the sum of the other two: $AC < 5 + 8 = 13$. It can come close to 13 but never reach it.

questions.stem:
The numbers in set $X$ have a standard deviation of $4$. Each number in $X$ is multiplied by $3$ and then increased by $5$ to form set $Y$.

**Quantity A:** The standard deviation of the numbers in $Y$

**Quantity B:** $12$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant does not change spread; multiplying by 3 multiplies the standard deviation by 3. So $3 \times 4 = 12$.

questions.stem:
$n$ is an integer.

**Quantity A:** The remainder when $n^2$ is divided by $4$

**Quantity B:** $1$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: If $n$ is odd, $n^2$ leaves remainder $1$ (for example $9 = 2 \times 4 + 1$); if $n$ is even, $n^2$ is a multiple of $4$ and leaves remainder $0$. Without knowing whether $n$ is odd, the comparison cannot be determined.

questions.stem: If $2^{x+3} = 32^{x-1}$, what is the value of $x$?
A committee of 3 people is to be chosen from a group of 7 people. How many different committees are possible? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: Order does not matter: $\binom{7}{3} = \frac{7 \times 6 \times 5}{3 \times 2 \times 1} = 35$. Counting ordered choices gives $210$, which counts each committee 6 times.

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle have lengths 6 and 10. Which of the following could be the length of the third side? Indicate all such lengths.
questions.explanation: The third side must be greater than $10 - 6 = 4$ and less than $10 + 6 = 16$. So $5$, $12$ and $15$ work; $4$ and $16$ would make a flat triangle.

questions.stem: The price of a stock rose 20 percent on Monday and fell 20 percent on Tuesday. Its price at the close on Tuesday was what percent of its price at the open on Monday?
questions.explanation: $1.2 \times 0.8 = 0.96$, so the price ended at 96 percent of where it began. The 20 percent fall is taken from the higher Monday price, so the changes do not cancel.

questions.stem: The ratio of men to women in a group is 3 to 5. After 8 more men join the group, the numbers of men and women are equal. How many women are in the group?
questions.explanation: Let the group have $3k$ men and $5k$ women. Then $3k + 8 = 5k$, so $k = 4$ and there are $5 \times 4 = 20$ women. $12$ is the original number of men.

questions.stem: A circle is inscribed in a square with sides of length 10. What is the area of the region inside the square but outside the circle, rounded to the nearest whole number? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: The circle's diameter is $10$, so $r = 5$ and its area is $25\pi \approx 78.54$. The square's area is $100$, leaving $100 - 78.54 = 21.46$, or $21$.

questions.stem: The average (arithmetic mean) of 6 numbers is 15. When one of the numbers is removed, the average of the remaining 5 numbers is 14. What number was removed?
questions.explanation: The 6 numbers sum to $90$ and the remaining 5 sum to $70$, so the removed number is $90 - 70 = 20$. The averages differ by only 1, but the totals differ by 20.

questions.stem: What is the greatest prime factor of $2^{10} - 1$?
questions.explanation: $2^{10} - 1 = 1023 = 3 \times 341 = 3 \times 11 \times 31$. $33$ is a factor but not prime.

questions.stem:
A university's enrollment, by college, is shown below.

| College | Students |
|---|---|
| Arts | 2,400 |
| Science | 3,600 |
| Business | 1,800 |
| Engineering | 2,200 |

If enrollment in Science rises by 25 percent and the other colleges are unchanged, what percent of total enrollment will be in Science, to the nearest percent?
questions.explanation: Science becomes $3{,}600 \times 1.25 = 4{,}500$ and the total becomes $10{,}000 + 900 = 10{,}900$. $\frac{4{,}500}{10{,}900} \approx 41.3\%$. Forgetting that the total also grows gives $45\%$.

questions.stem: If $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$ and $x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0$, what is the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: The first equation factors as $(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0$ and the second as $(x - 3)(x - 4) = 0$. The only value satisfying both is $3$.

questions.stem: Once a thriving port, the town has become so _____ that its single remaining hotel opens only in the summer.
questions.explanation: "Once a thriving port" signals decline, and a lone hotel that opens only in summer shows how few people there are: depopulated. Prosperous and congested describe the busy past, not the present.

questions.stem: Far from _____ the controversy, the minister's attempt at clarification only drew more attention to the remarks she had hoped people would forget.
questions.explanation: "Far from" sets up the opposite of what happened. Her clarification drew more attention, so it did the opposite of calming the controversy: defusing. Inflaming and prolonging describe what actually happened, so they remove the contrast.

questions.stem: The economist's forecasts have been [[1]] in recent years, missing nearly every major turn in the market, yet her reputation remains oddly [[2]], sustained more by her confident manner than by her record.
questions.explanation: Forecasts that missed nearly every turn are unreliable, the opposite of prescient. "Yet" and "oddly" signal that her reputation survived anyway: intact.

questions.stem: The garden designer prized [[1]] over display: her plantings were chosen to [[2]] the surrounding landscape rather than to compete with it, so that visitors often failed to notice where the garden ended and the [[3]] hillside began.
questions.explanation: A designer who prized the opposite of display valued subtlety. Plantings that do not compete with the landscape blend into it. If visitors cannot tell where the garden ends, the neighboring hillside must look natural too, so it is uncultivated rather than manicured.

questions.stem: The passage is chiefly concerned with
options: explaining why serialized adventure stories became popular in the 1850s
criticizing library committees that refused to buy the novels and adventure stories workers wanted
showing how library users' choices diverged from what the libraries' founders intended
describing how historians first discovered the borrowing records of early libraries
arguing that reading fiction made workers more skilled and content
questions.explanation: The founders wanted workers to read history and science; the records show they borrowed mostly fiction, and committees had to respond. The passage does not single out committees for criticism: it notes that some limited novels and others bought them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, some library committees responded to borrowers' preferences by
options: closing libraries that lent mostly fiction
charging borrowers a fee for each novel
requiring borrowers to read history before fiction
buying the books that borrowers asked for
questions.explanation: The passage says some committees "decided that any reading was better than none and bought what was asked for". Others limited purchases of novels, which is not the same as banning a kind of story or closing a library.

questions.stem:
The new manager was known for her _____: she answered every email within the hour and never missed a deadline.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Quick replies and met deadlines show that she could be counted on: reliability and dependability. Creativity and ingenuity are a pair, but the examples say nothing about original thinking.

questions.stem:
The documentary avoids _____ treatment of its subject, presenting the factory's closure through interviews that show the town's grief without dwelling on it.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Showing grief "without dwelling on it" means the film avoids excessive sentimentality: maudlin and mawkish. Dispassionate and detached are a pair, but the film does show grief, so it is not avoiding feeling altogether.

questions.stem:
His apology, offered only after the evidence against him had become _____, convinced few people of its sincerity.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: An apology that comes only once denial is impossible looks forced, which is why few believed it: incontrovertible and indisputable. Ambiguous and doubtful evidence would leave room for denial and would not explain the skepticism.

questions.passage: To reduce traffic in its town center, Elsby added a toll to the main bridge into the center last year. Since then, the number of cars crossing the bridge on weekdays has fallen by 15 percent. The town council concluded that the toll has reduced traffic in the town center.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the council's conclusion?
options: Whether drivers began reaching the town center by other routes that have no toll
Whether most of the drivers who pay the toll live outside the town of Elsby
Whether the toll is higher than the tolls charged on other bridges in the region
Whether the toll has raised more money than the council predicted it would
Whether weekend traffic on the bridge has fallen by as much as weekday traffic
questions.explanation: Fewer cars on the bridge means less traffic in the center only if those drivers did not simply switch to other routes into the center. How much the toll raises or how it compares with other tolls says nothing about traffic in the center.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true of lactase persistence? Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.
options: It is found in populations with a long history of herding animals.
It results from the same mutation wherever it occurs.
It arose more than once in human history.
questions.explanation: The trait "arose independently in several regions", among peoples who herded cattle, goats or camels. It arose "through different mutations", which rules out a single mutation.

questions.stem: The author uses the phrase "a textbook example" primarily to indicate that
options: the evidence for the case comes mainly from older studies
the case clearly illustrates a general evolutionary pattern
the debate about the selective pressure has been settled
the case is widely taught but poorly understood by researchers
the trait is found in most of the world's human populations
questions.explanation: The phrase introduces the case as a clear instance of convergent evolution: similar pressures, similar outcomes, different routes. The author immediately says the pressure "remains debated", so the debate has not been settled.

questions.stem: After a week of heavy rain, the usually _____ stream had become a torrent that swept away the footbridge.
questions.explanation: "Usually" contrasts the stream's normal state with the torrent, so normally it is calm: placid. Turbulent describes the torrent, not the usual stream.

questions.stem: The professor's lectures were so _____ that students often left the hall unsure what the main point had been.
questions.explanation: Students lost the main point because the lectures wandered: rambling. Concise or brief lectures would make the point easier to find.

questions.stem: Although the candidate claimed to be _____ about the outcome of the vote, aides reported that she had checked the early returns every few minutes.
questions.explanation: "Although" contrasts her claim with checking the returns every few minutes, so she claimed not to care: indifferent. Anxious fits her behavior, which removes the contrast.

questions.stem: The restaurant's menu is [[1]], offering only five dishes, but each is prepared with such [[2]] that diners rarely miss a wider choice.
questions.explanation: Five dishes is a limited menu. Diners do not miss more choice because each dish is excellent, which requires care, not haste.

questions.stem: Initially [[1]] by the plan's cost, the board eventually approved it once engineers showed that it would [[2]] maintenance expenses over the next decade.
questions.explanation: "Initially" and "eventually approved" mean the cost first put the board off: deterred. What won approval was a saving, so the plan would reduce maintenance expenses.

questions.stem: The passage mainly discusses
options: why critics opposed converting traffic lanes into bus lanes
how changes in road capacity affect the amount of driving people do
how traffic congestion affects the choice of jobs and homes
why buses and trains are more efficient than private cars
how planners design new highways for growing cities
questions.explanation: The first paragraph explains induced demand from wider roads; the second explains the reverse when roads are narrowed. Job and home choices appear only as one example of how people respond.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is one way that people respond to a newly widened road?
options: By combining several errands into a single trip
By taking trips that they would previously have skipped
By using buses and trains more often than before
By traveling at less busy times of the day
By moving closer to the places where they work
questions.explanation: The passage lists taking trips they would otherwise have skipped. Combining errands and traveling at other times are responses to a road being narrowed, and people switch away from buses and trains, not toward them.

questions.stem: The phrase "run in reverse" refers to the idea that
options: wider roads eventually become narrower as cities grow
bus lanes create more congestion than they relieve
reducing road capacity can reduce the total amount of traffic
drivers avoid roads that have recently been widened
traffic always returns to a road after it is reopened
questions.explanation: Extra capacity creates traffic; the reverse is that less capacity makes some traffic "simply vanish". The passage says the traffic does not all reappear elsewhere, which contradicts the idea that traffic always returns.

questions.stem:
The child's _____ questions, one after another all afternoon, exhausted even his patient grandmother.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Questions "one after another all afternoon" never stopped: ceaseless and endless. Occasional and rare are a pair but would not exhaust anyone.

questions.stem:
Critics found the sequel _____, a weaker copy of the original that added nothing new.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: "A weaker copy that added nothing new" defines derivative and unoriginal. Innovative and groundbreaking form a pair with the opposite meaning.

questions.stem:
Though the treaty ended the fighting, relations between the two countries remained _____ for decades, marked by mutual suspicion.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Relations "marked by mutual suspicion" were strained and tense. Cordial and friendly are a pair but contradict the suspicion.

questions.passage: Sales of electric bicycles at Rindel Cycles doubled in the year after the store began offering free test rides. The store's owner concluded that the test rides were responsible for the increase.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the owner's conclusion?
options: Rindel Cycles also sells ordinary bicycles, and their sales rose slightly in the same year.
The test rides took place on a short marked course in the parking lot behind the store, not on public roads.
Most customers who took a test ride at Rindel Cycles were already planning to buy a bicycle.
Electric bicycles cost more than most of the other bicycles sold at Rindel Cycles.
In the same year, electric bicycle sales doubled at stores in the region that offered no test rides.
questions.explanation: If stores without test rides saw the same doubling, something else, such as a regional trend, explains the rise. Customers already planning to buy is tempting, but it says nothing about whether test rides persuaded them to buy at Rindel.

questions.stem: According to the passage, most of an octopus's neurons are located
questions.explanation: "About two thirds lie in its eight arms." The passage says explicitly that most are not in the brain.

questions.stem: The example of the separated arm is used primarily to show that
options: the octopus brain is too small to control the movements of eight arms
an octopus arm can carry out complex actions without direction from the brain
an octopus arm finds food more quickly than the octopus's eyes do
the brain sets the goals that each arm then carries out
an octopus can regrow an arm after losing it to a predator
questions.explanation: A detached arm still reaches for food and passes it toward the mouth, so the arm can act on its own. That the brain sets the goals is a claim the passage makes, but the separated arm illustrates the arm's independence, not the brain's role.

questions.passage: A study of 2,000 adults found that those who ate breakfast every day weighed less, on average, than those who regularly skipped it. A nutrition website concluded that eating breakfast causes people to weigh less.
questions.stem: The website's conclusion is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: assumes that the people who skipped breakfast ate more food later in the day
relies on a study with too few participants to support any general conclusion about adults and their weight
fails to say what the people in the study ate for breakfast each morning
treats an average weight as though it applied to every person in the study
overlooks the possibility that breakfast eaters differ from skippers in other habits that affect weight
questions.explanation: A correlation between breakfast and weight does not show cause: breakfast eaters may also exercise more or eat differently. Two thousand adults is a substantial sample, so the sample-size criticism is weak.

questions.stem: The author's reputation for _____ is belied by her letters, which reveal a writer who agonized over every comma and rewrote some paragraphs dozens of times.
questions.explanation: "Belied" means shown to be false. Letters showing agonized rewriting contradict a reputation for writing with ease: facility. Perfectionism is what the letters reveal, so it would be confirmed, not belied.

questions.stem: The committee's report, though _____ in tone, contained recommendations radical enough to alarm the very officials who had commissioned it.
questions.explanation: "Though" contrasts the tone with alarming content, so the tone was bland and inoffensive: anodyne. Strident, incendiary, polemical and alarmist would all match the radical content rather than contrast with it.

questions.stem: The historian's account is [[1]] rather than comprehensive: she treats a handful of episodes in great depth and passes over others that conventional surveys consider [[2]].
questions.explanation: "Rather than comprehensive" and "a handful of episodes" point to selective. The episodes she skips are notable only if other surveys treat them as essential: indispensable. Passing over peripheral episodes would be unremarkable.

questions.stem: The orchestra's new conductor takes a(n) [[1]] approach to tempo, refusing to [[2]] the markings in the score even when tradition favors a slower reading; to some listeners the results sound [[3]], to others merely faithful.
questions.explanation: Refusing to depart from the score's markings is a scrupulous approach. Since tradition is slower than the markings, listeners used to tradition hear the faithful tempo as rushed. Idiosyncratic would clash with "merely faithful".

questions.stem: That the experiment's results were [[1]] did not trouble the investigators, who had designed it less to confirm a hypothesis than to [[2]] the range of possibilities worth testing.
questions.explanation: Results that might trouble investigators but did not, because confirmation was never the aim, were inconclusive. An exploratory experiment is meant to narrow the possibilities worth testing next.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole is concerned mainly with
options: tracing how photography gained admission to museums
defending early critics of photography against recent scholars
comparing scientific and artistic uses of early photography
challenging a conventional account of a medium's early history
explaining how photographic techniques for astronomy were developed
questions.explanation: The first paragraph sets out the standard story; the second reports scholarship that questions it and explains why critics invented the rivalry. Comparing the two uses is part of the evidence, not the purpose.

questions.stem: The example of methods for photographing faint stars serves primarily to
options: support the claim that techniques crossed between scientific and artistic photography
explain why portrait photographers preferred softer light
show that astronomers were the first photographers to produce exhibition prints
illustrate the rivalry between scientific and artistic photographers
suggest that portrait photographers depended on astronomers for their cameras and other equipment
questions.explanation: The example follows "techniques moved freely between the two" and shows a scientific method adopted by portraitists. It undercuts the rivalry rather than illustrating it.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the author suggest about the "later critics"? Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.
options: They opposed photography's admission to museums.
They exaggerated the separation between scientific and artistic photography.
Their account reflected concerns of their own time.
questions.explanation: The critics' need for a narrative "says more about the critics' own debates", and the rivalry was "largely a creation" of theirs. Their story ends with photography's triumph as art, so nothing suggests they opposed its admission to museums.

questions.stem:
Her colleagues regarded her habit of questioning every assumption not as _____ but as a form of rigor, though newcomers sometimes found it exasperating.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: The contrast is with rigor: the habit could be mistaken for opposing things for the sake of it, which is contrariness or perversity. Credulity and gullibility are a pair but describe the opposite of questioning everything.

questions.stem:
The memoir's _____ style, all short declarative sentences, suits a writer who distrusts eloquence.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: Short declarative sentences from someone who distrusts eloquence make a spare style: laconic and terse. Florid and ornate form a pair with the opposite meaning.

questions.stem:
What the agency described as a temporary measure proved remarkably _____, remaining in force for more than thirty years.

Select the two words that complete the sentence and give it the same meaning.
questions.explanation: A "temporary" measure lasting thirty years was durable and enduring. Ephemeral and fleeting match "temporary", which the sentence says proved wrong.

questions.passage: In regions where a certain pesticide was widely used, populations of a native frog species declined sharply over ten years. In regions where the pesticide was rarely used, populations of the same species remained stable. Researchers concluded that the pesticide is harmful to the frogs.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?
options: In laboratory tests, frog eggs exposed to the pesticide at levels found in treated regions hatched at much lower rates than unexposed eggs.
Regions where the pesticide is widely used also have more roads and new housing than regions where it is rarely used, and both have expanded quickly there over the same ten years.
Farmers in regions with heavy pesticide use report seeing fewer frogs in their fields than they did ten years ago.
The frog species is found in only a few regions, most of which are used for farming of some kind.
The pesticide breaks down within a few weeks of being applied to crops in warm weather.
questions.explanation: The laboratory result shows a direct harm at realistic exposure, ruling out other explanations for the field pattern. More roads and housing in pesticide regions offers a rival cause, which weakens the conclusion; farmers' reports only repeat the decline.

questions.passage: {{For centuries, sailors navigated by dead reckoning, estimating their position from a ship's speed, heading and the time elapsed.}} {{The method's weakness was that small errors in any of these quantities added up over a long voyage.}} {{Latitude could be checked by measuring the height of the sun at noon, but longitude required knowing the exact time at a reference port.}} {{A clock that kept accurate time at sea therefore became the most sought-after navigational instrument of the eighteenth century.}} {{Early marine clocks were expensive, and many ships went on relying on dead reckoning for decades after such clocks became available.}}
questions.stem: Select the sentence in the passage that explains why errors in dead reckoning grew worse on longer voyages.
questions.explanation: The second sentence says small errors "added up over a long voyage", which is why longer voyages meant larger errors. The third sentence explains why longitude was hard to fix, not why errors accumulated.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that sulfur droplets in the lower atmosphere
options: warm the surface by trapping heat from the sun
are produced mainly by human activity rather than by volcanoes
reflect more sunlight than droplets in the stratosphere do
would be removed more quickly than droplets in the stratosphere
last two or three years before they are washed out
questions.explanation: The stratosphere "has no rain to wash the droplets out", which is why droplets there linger far longer than particles lower down. The two-to-three-year figure applies to the stratosphere, not the lower atmosphere.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the overall effect of a large explosive eruption on global temperature over the following few years is most likely
options: cooling at first, followed by stronger warming once the droplets fall
warming, because sulfur droplets trap heat near the surface
warming, because the eruption releases carbon dioxide into the air
no change, because the cooling and warming effects cancel exactly
cooling, because reflective droplets outweigh the eruption's carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Large eruptions "can cool it for several years", and the eruption's carbon dioxide has only a "minor" warming effect. Nothing suggests a later warming stronger than the cooling.

questions.stem:
**Quantity A:** $\frac{5}{6}$

**Quantity B:** $\frac{6}{7}$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $\frac{5}{6} = \frac{35}{42}$ and $\frac{6}{7} = \frac{36}{42}$, so Quantity B is greater.

questions.stem:
$a$ and $b$ are positive and $a > b$.

**Quantity A:** $\frac{a}{b}$

**Quantity B:** $\frac{b}{a}$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Since $a > b > 0$, $\frac{a}{b} > 1$ and $\frac{b}{a} < 1$, so Quantity A is greater.

questions.stem:
A square and an equilateral triangle each have a perimeter of $24$.

**Quantity A:** The area of the square

**Quantity B:** The area of the triangle

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The square has side $6$ and area $36$. The triangle has side $8$ and area $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 64 = 16\sqrt{3} \approx 27.7$.

questions.stem:
A fair coin is tossed 3 times.

**Quantity A:** The probability of getting exactly 2 heads

**Quantity B:** The probability of getting exactly 1 head

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, 3 have exactly two heads (HHT, HTH, THH) and 3 have exactly one (HTT, THT, TTH). Both probabilities are $\frac{3}{8}$.

questions.stem: If 12 pencils cost \$3.60, how much do 30 pencils cost at the same price per pencil?
questions.explanation: Each pencil costs $3.60 \div 12 = 0.30$, so 30 pencils cost $30 \times 0.30 = 9.00$ dollars.

questions.stem: If $\frac{x}{4} + \frac{x}{6} = 5$, what is the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: Multiply by 12: $3x + 2x = 60$, so $5x = 60$ and $x = 12$.

questions.stem: The measures of the angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the measure, in degrees, of the largest angle? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: The parts total $2 + 3 + 4 = 9$, so one part is $180 \div 9 = 20$ degrees and the largest angle is $4 \times 20 = 80$.

questions.stem: Which of the following are prime numbers? Indicate all such numbers.
questions.explanation: $51 = 3 \times 17$, $57 = 3 \times 19$ and $91 = 7 \times 13$. $53$ and $59$ have no divisor up to their square roots (about 7.3 and 7.7), so they are prime.

questions.stem:
The table shows monthly rainfall at a weather station.

| Month | Rainfall (mm) |
|---|---|
| January | 40 |
| February | 55 |
| March | 70 |
| April | 35 |

By what percent did rainfall decrease from March to April?
questions.explanation: The decrease is $70 - 35 = 35$ mm, and $\frac{35}{70} = 50\%$. Dividing by April's value gives $100\%$, which measures an increase from April to March.

questions.stem: The average (arithmetic mean) score of 10 students on a quiz is 70. The 4 boys in the group have an average score of 64. What is the average score of the 6 girls?
questions.explanation: Total $= 10 \times 70 = 700$; the boys scored $4 \times 64 = 256$; the girls scored $444$, so their average is $444 \div 6 = 74$.

questions.stem: A driver travels 120 kilometers at an average speed of 60 kilometers per hour and returns along the same route at an average speed of 40 kilometers per hour. What is the average speed, in kilometers per hour, for the whole round trip?
questions.explanation: The trip out takes 2 hours and the return 3 hours, so $240$ km in $5$ hours is $48$ km per hour. Averaging the two speeds ($50$) ignores the longer time spent at the slower speed.

questions.stem: A rectangular garden 12 meters by 9 meters is surrounded by a path 1 meter wide. What is the area of the path, in square meters?
questions.explanation: The garden and path together measure $14 \times 11 = 154$. Subtract the garden, $12 \times 9 = 108$: the path is $46$. Adding only one meter to each dimension gives $13 \times 10 - 108 = 22$, a common slip.

questions.stem:
**Quantity A:** $2^5$

**Quantity B:** $5^2$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $2^5 = 32$ and $5^2 = 25$, so Quantity A is greater.

questions.stem:
$x + y = 10$ and $x - y = 4$

**Quantity A:** $x$

**Quantity B:** $7$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Adding the equations gives $2x = 14$, so $x = 7$.

questions.stem:
A circle has a radius of $3$.

**Quantity A:** The circumference of the circle

**Quantity B:** $19$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The circumference is $2\pi(3) = 6\pi \approx 18.85$, which is less than $19$.

questions.stem:
In a group of 40 people, 25 percent are left-handed.

**Quantity A:** The number of left-handed people in the group

**Quantity B:** $8$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: 25 percent of 40 is $10$, which is greater than $8$.

questions.stem:
$x^2 = 16$

**Quantity A:** $x$

**Quantity B:** $4$

Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: $x$ can be $4$ or $-4$, so $x$ may equal $4$ or be less than it.

questions.stem: What is the value of $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{9}{10}$?
questions.explanation: $\frac{2 \times 9}{3 \times 10} = \frac{18}{30} = \frac{3}{5}$. Adding numerators and denominators ($\frac{11}{13}$) is not multiplication.

questions.stem: A shirt costs \$25 after a 20 percent discount. What was the original price, in dollars? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: The sale price is 80 percent of the original: $0.8p = 25$, so $p = 31.25$. Adding 20 percent to \$25 gives \$30, which is wrong because the discount was taken from the original price.

questions.stem: If $4x + 3 = 27$, what is the value of $2x$?
questions.explanation: $4x = 24$, so $x = 6$ and $2x = 12$. Stopping at $x = 6$ answers a different question.

questions.stem: The area of a square is 49. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: The side is $\sqrt{49} = 7$, so the perimeter is $4 \times 7 = 28$.

questions.stem: What is the median of the numbers 3, 8, 1, 9, 4 and 7?
questions.explanation: In order: 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9. With six values the median is the average of the middle two: $\frac{4 + 7}{2} = 5.5$. The mean is about $5.3$.

questions.stem: An integer is chosen at random from the integers 1 through 10. Which of the following events have a probability of exactly $\frac{1}{2}$? Indicate all such events.
options: The integer is a multiple of 3.
questions.explanation: Even, odd and greater than 5 each cover 5 of the 10 integers. There are 4 primes (2, 3, 5, 7) and 3 multiples of 3, giving $\frac{4}{10}$ and $\frac{3}{10}$.

questions.stem: A worker earns \$18 an hour for the first 40 hours she works in a week and 1.5 times that rate for each additional hour. How much does she earn in a week in which she works 46 hours?
questions.explanation: Regular pay: $40 \times 18 = 720$. Overtime rate: $1.5 \times 18 = 27$, so 6 extra hours earn $162$. Total \$882. Paying all 46 hours at the higher rate gives \$1,242.

questions.stem: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of length 13 and one leg of length 5. What is the area of the triangle? Type the number only.
questions.explanation: The other leg is $\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$, so the area is $\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 12 = 30$.

questions.stem: In a survey of 200 people, 45 percent prefer tea, 35 percent prefer coffee and the rest prefer neither. How many of the people surveyed prefer neither?
questions.explanation: The rest is $100 - 45 - 35 = 20$ percent, and 20 percent of 200 is $40$.

questions.stem: The quantity $y$ varies directly with $x$, and $y = 12$ when $x = 3$. What is the value of $y$ when $x = 7$?
